name: Example: Determining a Minimum Possible Value Using the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
problem: Consider the vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14046175/assets/d1a095e61e6ea64f97a105fd69bc07f3f44990cd6d9794e54e355463c37a2413.png) Given that $\mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v}=-12$ and $\Vert \mathbf{v}\Vert =4,$ what is the smallest possible value of $k?$
worked_solution:
We will use the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

$$
\vert \mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v} \vert \leq \Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert \cdot \Vert \mathbf{v} \Vert.
$$

We are given all the quantities in the inequality above, except for $\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert.$ So first, we compute $\Vert \mathbf{u} \Vert$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖u‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{k})^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6+k}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|u\cdot v| & \le ‖u‖\cdot ‖v‖ \\ |-12| & \le \sqrt{6+k}\cdot (4) \\ 12 & \le 4\sqrt{6+k} \\ 3 & \le \sqrt{6+k} \\ {3}^{2} & \le (\sqrt{6+k})^{2} \\ 9 & \le 6+k \\ 3 & \le k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the smallest possible value of $k$ is $3.$
